hints: Focus on rate, not position of equilibrium. Temperature changes kinetic energy of all particles, not just one direction.
Recall that a higher temperature means more molecules have energy greater than $E_a$ for both the forward exothermic step and the backward endothermic step.
Think about which rate increases more to cause the equilibrium shift, while remembering that both individual rates still go up.
walkthrough:
**Separate Rate From Equilibrium**

Think like a teacher with two ideas in your head. Kinetics asks how fast, equilibrium asks where it ends up. This question asks about rates.

Reaction: $$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g) \quad \Delta H = -92 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

**Apply Temperature To Kinetics**

When temperature rises, all particles gain kinetic energy. More collisions are successful in both directions because more particles exceed activation energy.

Rate rule: $$\text{higher T} \rightarrow \text{more particles with } E > E_a \rightarrow \text{faster rate}$$

**Explain The Equilibrium Shift**

Both rates increase, but not equally. The backward endothermic decomposition of $\text{NH}_3$ has the larger $E_a$, so its rate increases more. That is why the equilibrium shifts left, even though the forward rate also increased.

options.A: Correct. Increasing temperature supplies kinetic energy to all reactants and products, so both forward and backward reaction rates increase. The backward rate increases more, shifting equilibrium left, but the forward rate still increases too.
options.B: Incorrect. This confuses the net equilibrium shift with individual rates. It is true the equilibrium shifts backward (to the left) because the reaction is exothermic, but the forward rate does not stay the same or decrease, it also increases.
options.C: Incorrect. This is the opposite confusion. Students sometimes think because heat favours ammonia formation at low temperature, heating must speed up only the forward reaction. In fact heating speeds up both, and favours the backward direction overall.
options.D: Incorrect. Temperature always affects rate because it changes particle kinetic energy and the fraction exceeding $E_a$. Saying no effect ignores collision theory and the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution.
